claim: When an idempotent ingest resolves a primary-key collision by reading the stored row back, a failure of that read must be reported as a retryable internal error, never as a payload conflict, because a conflict verdict tells the client to mint a new id for an event that is already recorded and double-counts spend.
because: LightTrack batch ingest .ok().flatten()-ed the read-back and reported store failures as `conflict: different payload`; fixed in e26d6cb and verified with the api suite (217 tests). The single-event door already propagated the error - the two doors had drifted on exactly the retry semantics the technique exists to protect.

claim: When a write API accepts a boolean control (enabled, locked, frozen), grep for its readers before trusting it: a flag with a setter, a column and a display but no enforcement site is a label, and the fix is to route it through the same cache/path the feature's other per-row policy already uses.
because: LightTrack's Project.enabled was accepted by PUT /v1/projects/:id, persisted by all three stores and shown in listings, and read by nothing on the ingest or auth path; a disabled project's keys kept ingesting. Fixed in aa1b2aa by widening the existing per-project redaction-policy cache into a project-policy cache and checking it on both ingest doors; the grep that found it (`\.enabled` across the API crate) took one call.

claim: When an incremental usage cache folds rows inside a transaction, a rollback must reset the cache (or restore its insertion cursor), because a store that reuses insertion ids after rollback will hand the freed ids to the next events and the advanced cursor makes them invisible - an under-count, not the over-count the naive reading expects.
because: LightTrack SQLite batch admission: `events.id` is TEXT so the implicit rowid is max+1 and a rolled-back batch frees it; the cache's `seen_rowid` stayed past it. A test drove the rollback, proved the rowid reuse, and read $9 from the cache where the full-scan reference read $12. Fixed in ba63d35 by resetting the cache on commit failure. The technique text covers eviction and exactness but says nothing about the fold running inside a transaction that can fail.

claim: when an alert carries a delta a counter has already discarded (a periodic flush of rejected calls), its dedup key must include the flush instant, because a cooldown that suppresses the second flush deletes the only copy of that delta
because: lighttrack: ingest-rejected flushes at 900s under a 3600s cooldown lost 3 of every 4 deltas (store answered Suppressed, no row); fixed by keying on the flush timestamp, pinned by a store-backed test

claim: a multi-tenant HTTP API's credential boundary is its own subject: bearer-key minting (prefix + salted digest, shown once), constant-time compare via fixed-width digests, failed-attempt throttling keyed on a trusted source identity, key capabilities narrower than the tenant, expiry as a distinct code from a wrong guess, a tenant kill switch enforced at the credential, and a scope carried on every store read so a foreign id is not-found rather than forbidden
because: lighttrack: crates/api/src/{auth,guards,auth_scopes,auth_throttle}.rs implement all of these and the registry joined the context to agent-cli-transport / client-state (homonyms); three rounds of findings here (enforced-without-admin-key lockout, per-request last_used write, unpinned error-code contract) had no technique to be judged against

claim: a normalized token-usage record must state whether cached input is a SUBSET of input or ADDITIONAL to it, and every per-provider extractor must convert to that one convention - OpenAI's prompt_tokens includes cached tokens, Anthropic's input_tokens excludes cache_read_input_tokens - or the price book bills the same cache hit two different ways
because: lighttrack: PriceBook::cost_usd_mode computes billable_input = input - cached (subset convention); the Python, Rust and TS Anthropic extractors pass input_tokens through unchanged, so an Anthropic call with input_tokens=1000 and cache_read=800 bills 200 uncached instead of 1000 - the wire type's doc says only 'provider-dependent'

claim: When a per-call generation knob is encoded as a suffix on the model string, split it off at the ONE boundary every adapter crosses, never inside the adapters - one adapter will parse it and the rest will forward it into the provider's model field.
because: Measured in tracklight: split_effort had exactly one caller (the CLI adapter) out of four generation paths. The default judge spec was opus@xhigh and the preferred Anthropic route was the bare Messages API, which passed the whole suffixed string as a model id. Fixed by splitting in generate_once above every adapter, with a per-adapter test asserting no '@' reaches the wire model field.

claim: A defect on a provider path can hide behind CREDENTIAL SHAPE, not just behind a rare input: whichever auth the developer's own environment uses is the path that gets exercised, so a bug can fire on every deployment configured as documented and never once locally.
because: The suffixed-model bug survived because this machine authenticates Anthropic through the CLI's subscription OAuth - the single adapter that stripped the suffix - while .env carried only Gemini/OpenAI keys. The broken path was the one the module's own doc calls preferred, reached by setting the API key the deployment docs tell you to set.

claim: An ORDER BY with no deterministic tie-break is a latent correctness bug wherever a reader takes 'the latest row', because adding an index can change which tied row comes first - the row order is a query-plan artifact, not data.
because: Landed in tracklight: adding idx_benchmark_runs_bench turned a table scan into an index walk and flipped which of two same-instant benchmark runs read as latest, moving a prompt-promotion gate from refuse to allow. Fixed with (started_at DESC, id DESC) - deterministic, and explicitly NOT a claim that one simultaneous run was later.

claim: A regression test for a plan-dependent ordering bug must be falsifiable against the FIX, not against a repeated read: two identical queries reuse one plan and agree with or without a tie-break, so a read-twice-and-compare test passes on the broken code.
because: Wrote exactly that test first and it passed on the unfixed code. Replaced it with one that inserts rows in an order disagreeing with the tie-break and asserts the pinned sequence, then verified it by deleting ', id DESC' and watching it fail. Same method caught a second, opposite error: a reported pricing bug whose fix was a no-op, proven because the test still passed after reverting the fix.

claim: Raising a token ceiling to permit deeper reasoning is a wall-clock decision as much as a token one: the request timeout must scale with the effort level, or 'think harder' becomes 'time out harder'.
because: tracklight maps xhigh/max onto output_config.effort and raises max_tokens to 64000 there, behind a process-wide 120s non-streaming HTTP timeout that had been measured against default-effort calls. Fixed with a per-request timeout keyed on effort - per-request because the client is shared, so widening it globally would hand a black-holed endpoint the same budget.

claim: A paired test must align on case IDENTITY, never on vector length - and a compacted per-case vector (one that skips failed cases rather than holding a gap) makes equal length a lie about equal case sets.
because: Landed in tracklight: two benchmark targets that each errored on a DIFFERENT case finished with equal-length score vectors, and the paired test zipped them by position. Two targets scoring identically on every case they both judged produced mean_delta 0.15 with p=0.0 and significant=true - a certain win manufactured out of a one-case offset. Fixed by carrying the case id in the score type and aligning on the intersection.

claim: Misaligned pairing is WORSE than an unpaired test, not merely weaker: differencing two different cases adds between-case variance to the deltas while the paired standard error still claims it was removed, so the verdict comes back wrong AND overconfident.
because: Measured on the tracklight fix: the misaligned pairing reported zero stderr and p=0.0 - maximal confidence - on a comparison that had no real gap at all. A tool that degrades to an unpaired test on mismatched sets would have been safer than one that silently paired by position.

claim: A test NAME can assert a guard the code never performed, and it hides the gap more effectively than a missing test - anyone grepping 'is this checked?' finds the name and stops.
because: tracklight had a test named paired_deltas_refuses_mismatched_case_sets guarding a function that only compared vector lengths. The name made the same overstatement as the doc comment, and both survived months of review. Renaming it to say what it does was part of the fix, not cosmetic.

claim: When verifying a test is falsifiable by breaking the code it guards, confirm the FILE ACTUALLY CHANGED before believing the result - a break that silently fails to apply produces a passing test that reads as proof of the opposite.
because: Happened twice in one session on tracklight, to a builder and to its reviewer independently. A string replacement with no assertion no-opped; the test passed; the momentary conclusion was that the guard was worthless. An assert on the replacement or a diff check costs nothing and separates a proof from a coincidence.

claim: When a statistical claim gains a caveat field, audit every RENDERER of that claim - a presentation layer that branches on significance will often print notes on the weak branch only, so the strongest sentence the tool emits becomes the one that cannot say what it rests on.
because: tracklight's winner_line returned early on significant claims and never printed caveats, so a best claim tested over a case-set intersection rendered as an unqualified winner. The layer is shared by the runner, the CLI and MCP, so a compensating stdout print in the runner reached one consumer of three.

claim: A tolerant parse that degrades an unknown enum to a default must not be shared between a READ path and a WRITE path: degrading is correct for deserialising stored rows (forward compatibility) and is silent data loss when accepting operator input.
because: tracklight shared one de_difficulty between both. POSTing a benchmark case with a tier off the closed ladder returned 200 and stored ungraded; a live 18-case run shipped 8 cases that way and the per-tier report then covered a corpus whose grading had been discarded. Fixed by strict validation at the API boundary with the deserialiser left tolerant, and one test pinning both halves together.

claim: When a benchmark gains a new axis or a graded field, add it to the machine-readable contract callers read - an axis absent from the schema is an axis nobody varies, and the omission fails silently by construction.
because: tracklight shipped reasoning-effort targets and graded difficulty tiers with tests and docs; both were absent from the JSON Schema an MCP agent receives for create_benchmark. Grep for effort in that file returned zero. That absence is why the first live run graded cases with a rung that does not exist.

claim: Report per-tier discrimination descriptively alongside the scorecard: a tier every target scored identically on separated nothing, and the operator is paying for it. State it as an observation, never as a significance test - per-tier power is far below the run's.
because: Measured in tracklight: a 6-target 9-case run spent 36 of 54 generation calls on two tiers that every target scored 1.00 on. The framework could not say so; the finding needed a hand-written script. After shipping the verdict a live run printed it unaided. Per-tier significance was deliberately NOT built - the discriminating tier in that run had three cases.

claim: Difficulty-for-humans is not difficulty-for-LLMs: classic cognitive-reflection traps make a useless benchmark tier because they are famous and in training data.
because: A live tracklight run graded bat-and-ball, 5-machines and lily-pads as a medium tier. All six model/effort configurations scored 100% on every one of them. The tier separated nothing and cost a third of the run.

claim: Do not assume a cheaper model tier means a cheaper or faster call - measure per-case cost and latency, because a small model can burn far more reasoning tokens on a hard case than a large one.
because: Measured on the Claude CLI path: haiku at low effort cost 0.086 USD and took 142 seconds on a constraint puzzle that opus at high effort answered in 11 seconds for 0.085 USD - haiku emitted 15466 thinking tokens against opus's 445. Any frontier that ordered targets by assumed tier rather than measured cost would have got this backwards.

claim: An absent correlation statistic renders as a definite value: crates/render/src/labels.rs:139-141 formats opt_f(c, "pearson"|"mae"|"rmse").unwrap_or(0.0) as {:.3}, so a label set with no computed agreement shows 0.000 - and 0.000 is a meaningful reading for a correlation (no relationship), not a recognisable placeholder. opt_u(c, "n").unwrap_or(0) has the same shape one line above.
because: Found while applying the number-formatting amendment to traces.rs. The corpus already owns this under number-formatting's 'Zero, unknown, and too-small are three facts' and the law unknown-is-not-a-value; this tree already has the correct habit elsewhere (render/src/schedules.rs::every and three .map(|m| format!("{m}ms")).unwrap_or_else(|| "—") sites), so the fix is to follow the file's own convention, not to invent one. Not fixed in this run because the right sentinel for a numeric column that tooling may parse is a judgment the project owns.

claim: "Repair the shared layer, never the caller that noticed" is only half the rule: it does not say to REMOVE the caller-side patch once the shared repair lands. In this tree both survive. crates/render/src/compare.rs:21-25 documents the caveat as printed on both branches and emits it at :60; crates/runner/src/compare.rs:1134-1138 still prints the same string itself as a separate "BEST CLAIM — …" line, so the runner stdout carries the caveat twice — and its justifying comment at :1131 ("the render layer's winner line has no slot for a caveat on a claim it calls significant") now states the opposite of what the render layer does, which reads to the next reader as a standing, unfixed finding.
because: Found reading this pair for /conform. The technique names the wrong fix and the right one but stops at the moment the right one is made; the observed residue is not a second bug so much as the predictable tail of the prescribed repair — the caller-side print is invisible to every test (it is stdout, not the rendered artifact), and the comment that justified it is exactly the artifact a later reader trusts. Suggested addition to procedure step 5: after repairing the shared layer, delete the caller-side print and the comment that argued for it, because a duplicated caveat trains readers to skim it and a stale justification re-opens a closed finding.
